verify.backtranslation: It is false that every ordered pair of prime natural numbers p and q occurs as the greatest prime factors of consecutive natural numbers n and n+1 with n at least 2. Equivalently, some ordered pair of primes has no such n. A greatest prime factor here means a prime divisor at least as large as every prime divisor of the number.

issues: Uses the positive-integer domain implicit in the supplied resolution notes: P is defined only for n >= 2. If the word integer were instead interpreted to allow negative n and P(abs(n)), this proof would not resolve that different formulation (n=-8 realizes p=2,q=7). Independent statement review should explicitly confirm the intended positive domain.
faithful.verdict: Faithful to the positive-integer problem resolved by the supplied notes, with the domain interpretation explicitly qualified.

verify.backtranslation: There exist a nonnegative integer n and disjoint finite sets A and B of points in the real plane, with exactly n points in A and max(n-3, 0) points in B. The set A is not contained in any straight line. Every straight line containing two distinct points of A contains at least one point of B. Lines are represented by equations ax+by=c with real coefficients and at least one of a,b nonzero.

issues: Natural-number subtraction is truncated, but the noncollinearity condition excludes n below 3; the actual witness uses n=9.
faithful.verdict: This is precisely a counterexample to the asserted ordinary-line property, matching the disproof recorded in the resolution notes.

verify.backtranslation: Let r be a nonnegative integer, and consider r congruence classes with integer residues and positive integer moduli. If their union contains all 2^r integers s, s+1, ..., s+2^r-1 for some integer s, then their union contains every integer. Repeated moduli and residues are allowed.

faithful.verdict: The theorem proves the full stated covering implication for positive moduli, allowing repetitions and all integer starting points and targets.
